title: Investigation or close reading: the purpose of the Michigan Constitution
subject: social-studies
essentialQuestion: How can understanding Michigan's government and citizenship help us explain, decide, create, or solve something that matters?
successCriteria: I can say what a library record tells me about a document.
I can tell a fact in the record apart from a guess I added.
I can name one thing a record does not tell me.

vocabulary.definition: a written plan for how a government works
a library card that tells you about a document
something made at the time by people who were there
an idea you add that the source does not state

sourceIntegrity.policy: Every source here is a real repository record from the verified source set already bound to this canonical lesson. Record titles are reproduced from the repository catalog and are labeled as catalog titles, not as words spoken by a person. Plain-language restatements are labeled as paraphrases. No quotation, title, creator, date, or URL is invented, and no document text is reproduced.
sources: Library of Congress item 2022688639 (House message, December 10, 1835)
Library of Congress item 2022697426 (Senate message, December 10, 1835)
U.S. National Archives Milestone Documents, Constitution of the United States (1787)

sections.title: Question and context
sections.body:
Michigan has a constitution. A constitution is a written plan for how a government works.
Why would people sit down and write one?
Historians answer questions like that with evidence. Today your evidence is records. A record is like a library card for a document. It tells you who made the document, when, and what it is.
Your job is to say what a record tells you. You will also say what it does not tell you.

sections.title: Build background
sections.body:
Michigan was not always a state. First it was a territory.
In 1835 the people of Michigan wrote a constitution. They wanted Michigan to join the United States.
Congress had to agree first. Michigan became a state in 1837.
Libraries and archives keep records about those old documents. You are going to read three of those records today.

sections.title: EXAMPLE evidence — a record about the United States Constitution

source.repository: U.S. National Archives and Records Administration, Milestone Documents
source.what_this_is: A repository record. It describes a document. It is not the document's words.
source.note: The model below uses this United States record. Your own task uses two different records about Michigan.
source.limit: This record names the document and the year. It does not tell you what the Constitution says inside.

sections.title: EXAMPLE — how to read a record
sections.directions: Watch how the thinking goes. You do not answer here. Your turn comes after the Michigan records.

items.prompt: What does this record tell you about the document?

steps: Read the title first. It names the document: the Constitution of the United States.
Look for a date. The title gives the year 1787.
Look for where it is kept. The record says the National Archives.
Decide what kind of source it is. It was written in 1787 by people who were there, so it is a primary source.
Name one limit. The record does not tell you what the Constitution says inside.

items.prompt: Which part is a fact from the record, and which part is a guess?

steps: A fact is something the record actually states.
The record states the year 1787. Point to it. That is a fact from the record.
A guess is an idea you add that the record does not state.
Saying everyone agreed with the Constitution is a guess. The record never says that.
Keep the two apart, and say out loud which one you are giving.

sections.title: Look at evidence — the message to the House

source.record_title: Michigan -- Constitution, &c. -- state government. Message from the President of the United States, transmitting a constitution and form of government by the inhabitants of the Territory of Michigan, with a view to the admission of the said territory into the Union, on an equal footing with the original states. December 10, 1835. Read, and referred to a select committee
source.creator: United States Congress, House; message from President Andrew Jackson
source.record_note: These words are the title of the library record. They are not a quotation from a person.
source.paraphrase: Paraphrase: the President sent Michigan's constitution to the House. The people of the Michigan Territory had written it. Michigan asked to join the Union with the same standing as the older states.
source.limit: The record names the document and the day it was read. It does not tell you what the constitution says inside.

sections.title: Look at evidence — the message to the Senate

source.record_title: Message from the President of the United States, with a copy of the Constitution adopted by the people of Michigan for forming a state government, &c. December 10, 1835. Read, and ordered to be printed, and referred to a select committee
source.creator: United States Congress, Senate; message from President Andrew Jackson
source.record_note: These words are the title of the library record. They are not a quotation from a person.
source.paraphrase: Paraphrase: on the same day, a message went to the Senate with a copy of the constitution the people of Michigan had adopted.
source.limit: Two records can describe the same day. That does not mean the event happened twice.

sections.title: Your turn — what do the Michigan records tell you?
sections.directions: Read the two Michigan records again. Point to the words that give you your answer.

items.prompt: Which sentence is a fact stated in the two Michigan records?

choices.label: Both messages were read on December 10, 1835.
Everyone in Michigan wanted to join the United States.

feedback.correct: Yes. You can point to that date in both record titles, so it is a fact the records state.
feedback.incorrect: Go back and point to the words. The records give a date you can see, so that one is a fact. How people felt is not in the records, so that is a guess. And watch the years: 1835 is when the constitution was sent to Congress, not when Michigan became a state.

items.prompt: The records say the people of Michigan formed a constitution and a state government. What was Michigan asking Congress to do?

choices.label: Let Michigan join the Union as a state.
Draw a new map of the Great Lakes.
Choose a new President for the country.

feedback.correct: Right. The House record says the constitution was sent with a view to admission into the Union, so joining is the ask.
feedback.incorrect: Look in the House record for the word admission. Admission means being let in. Then ask yourself: let in to what? The record answers that in the same line. Maps and Presidents are not mentioned anywhere in either record.

items.prompt: Which one do these library records NOT tell you?

choices.label: What rules the Michigan constitution set down inside it.
The day the messages were read.

feedback.correct: Yes. A record is like a library card. It describes a document from the outside and stops there.
feedback.incorrect: Check each choice against the record. The day is printed in the title. The library is named in the record. But nowhere do these records copy out the rules inside the constitution, so that is the one they do not tell you.

sections.title: Feedback — what it says and what you guess
sections.body:
Some answers add ideas the record never states. That is a guess, not a fact.
Go back to the record. Put your finger on the words that gave you the answer. If you cannot point to any words, you are guessing.
Guessing is not bad. Historians guess all the time. They just say out loud that it is a guess, and then they go looking for more evidence.

items.prompt: Someone writes: "The people of Michigan were excited to join the Union." Is that a fact from the records, or a guess?

choices.label: A guess. The records do not say how people felt.
A fact. The records say they were excited.
A fact, because it sounds true.

feedback.correct: Yes. Try to point to a feeling word in either record. There is none, so this is a guess.
feedback.incorrect: Read both record titles again and hunt for a word about feelings. You will not find one. Sounding true is not the test. The test is whether you can point to the words in the source.

sections.title: Your turn — write what the records show
sections.directions: Write on your own. Use both Michigan records. You do not need the model any more.

items.prompt: What do the two 1835 records show about why the people of Michigan wrote a constitution? Name one thing the records do tell you. Then name one thing they do not tell you.

feedback.correct: You used the records instead of your memory, and you were honest about where they stop. That is how a historian writes.
feedback.incorrect: Build your answer in two parts. Part one: copy out one thing you can point to in a record, such as the date or the request to be admitted. Part two: name something the records leave out, such as the rules inside the constitution or how people felt about it.

reference.what_you_learned: A record tells you about a document from the outside: who made it, when, and what it is.
reference.evidence_you_used: Two Library of Congress records from December 10, 1835 about Michigan's constitution, and one National Archives record for the model.
reference.how_you_did: Trusted assessment will check whether you pointed to the records and kept facts apart from guesses.
reference.what_to_review: The difference between what a record states and what you added yourself.
reference.review_this_lesson: Read one record again and say one fact and one guess out loud before you reread your writing.

items.prompt: Review this lesson: pick your best next step.

choices.label: Continue. I pointed to the records and named a limit.
Read the two Michigan records once more before I continue.
Practise saying one fact and one guess out loud.

feedback.correct: Good choice. Naming your own next step is part of the work.
feedback.incorrect: Any of these three can be right for you. Pick the one that matches what you actually did, not the one that looks best.

whatYouLearned: A constitution is a written plan for how a government works.
A record tells you about a document: who made it, when, and what it is.
In 1835 the people of Michigan sent their constitution to Congress and asked to join the Union.
A fact is something the source states. A guess is something you added.
